source.title: Bayesian scaling laws for in-context learning
source.authors: Aryaman Arora; Daniel Jurafsky; Christopher Potts; Noah D. Goodman

record.file_problem: Full paper text and appendices are present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: Extends research on safety failures under in-context learning to real-world instruction-tuned LLMs and a HarmBench-based many-shot jailbreaking evaluation. It does not test the specific fine-tuning, token-position, or bypass interventions in the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The real-world HarmBench evaluation reports the probability of a fixed compliant-response prefix as shots increase, rather than a direct refusal or harmful-completion rate. The synthetic GINC SFT and DPO experiments use HMM task preferences, not safety behavior. The paper does not measure aligned-versus-base per-token KL, or test response prefills, adversarial suffixes, decoding changes, localized weights, or safety-deepening training.
record.test_reason: No claim version is tested. The safety experiment is many-shot in-context jailbreaking of instruct models, scored by the probability of a fixed compliant prefix ('Here is how'). That is not harmful or benign fine-tuning (V1/V2), aligned-versus-base per-token KL (V3), or prefill, suffix or decoding attacks (V4). It also covers no localization (V5), causes of shallowness (V6) or deepening (V7). The GINC SFT/DPO experiments use toy HMM task preferences, not safety behaviour. The paper cites Qi et al. 2024 (an original source) only in related work, on post-training being superficial. Its finding that alignment lowers the prior but leaves the behaviour learnable in-context is a related construct, so it is recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that instruction-tuning of Llama 3.1 8B reduces the prior probability of unsafe behaviours (HarmBench and three persona evals) but fails to prevent many-shot jailbreaking. The posterior from their Bayesian fit eventually saturates. With the toy SFT/DPO results, they read this as evidence that instruction-tuning modifies task priors, not task knowledge, possibly because post-training compute is small relative to pretraining. This rests on fitted scaling-law parameters and prefix probabilities, not on refusal rates.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies in-context learning curves and fits Bayesian scaling laws; its safety-related real-model experiment uses many-shot demonstrations rather than the fine-tuning, token-KL, or response-prefill methods in the original sources.
record.method_sensitivity: The evaluations vary shot count, model, and dataset; real-world prompts use each model's chat template and only the starting 90% of the context window.

fits_no_version.finding: Across 7 instruct LLMs (1B–405B), the probability of the compliant prefix 'Here is how' on HarmBench requests rises with the number of in-context harmful demonstrations (Fig. 20, curves only). In Llama 3.1 8B, Instruct starts with a lower prior on unsafe behaviour than Base, but its fitted posterior eventually saturates (Fig. 5). Table 13 gives fitted HarmBench in-distribution probability: Instruct 0.39 vs Base 0.85.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety instruction-tuning lowers the prior on harmful compliance but leaves it re-learnable via many-shot in-context demonstrations. Here this is measured as the probability of a compliant prefix, not a harmful-completion rate.

record.problems: The safety-related real-world measure is the probability of a fixed prefix, not a direct refusal or harmful-completion rate. The paper reports the key ICL curves as figures without tabulated values or uncertainty for this measure. Its synthetic SFT/DPO studies are on toy HMM tasks, not safety behavior.
record.rows_left_out: No additional HarmBench model-by-shot rows were reported numerically; the included figure-only rows preserve each model's plotted curve. Derived posterior parameters and scaling-law fit errors were left out because they are not direct measures of harmful behavior.

untested.parts: No fine-tuning of safety-trained models on harmful data.
No benign fine-tuning of safety-trained models.
No per-token KL between aligned and base models across response positions. The Base vs Instruct comparison concerns prefix probability under many-shot ICL, not position-wise divergence.

No response prefilling, adversarial suffixes or decoding changes. Many-shot demonstrations are a different attack. The compliant prefix is force-decoded only to score its probability, not to test whether getting past it yields harmful continuations.
No weight, neuron or rank localization.
No test of whether safety data or objective causes shallowness. The 'prior not knowledge' account comes from Bayesian fit parameters, not from varying the alignment data or objective.
No deepening or robustness training evaluated.

record.verdict_notes: The rows are correctly unlinked (versions none) and marked cannot_determine, since the values are figure-only. The Figure 5a caption notes Instruct shows better ICL overall 'except on harmbench'. The HarmBench NRMSE values in Table 11 are scaling-law fit quality, not safety measures, so leaving them out is correct. The fitted K and P_ii parameters (Tables 12–13) are derived fit quantities and were reasonably left out of the rows.

versions.untested_parts: No safety-trained model is fine-tuned on harmful examples to measure harmful compliance.
No benign instruction data is used to test changes in harmful compliance.
No aligned-versus-base per-token KL divergence on harmful prompts is measured.
The study tests many-shot in-context demonstrations, not prefilling a compliant response opening, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes as listed in this version.
No weight or rank localization of safety behavior is tested.
The study does not test whether safety-training data or objectives cause shallow safety behavior.
No training intended to deepen safety behavior, or its robustness, is evaluated.
